New research from Replit on scaling laws for agent swarms. 

We show that scaling the number of agents can yield dramatic performance gains, but unlike traditional scaling laws, more compute doesn't necessarily translate into better results, and how agents organize themselves matters.

- Given a fixed two-hour window, Opus 5.5 went from a 3.7x speedup on NumPy with one agent to 18.9x with 32 agents.

- GPT-6.2 Astra was the strongest solo agent but exhibited negative scaling beyond 8 agents.

- Models spontaneously developed different organizational structures. Decentralized swarms scaled better than those that relied on centralized coordination.

- The parallelizability of the problem was a strong predictor of swarm performance.

- Interestingly, individual model intelligence is a poor predictor of collective intelligence.

We’re also open-sourcing Optimization-Bench to advance research into this new dimension of inference-time scaling.

tweets.text:
Huge opportunity right now to build new services firms from the ground up, or transform existing ones, with agents at the center. 

The expertise that services firms in theory should have is as important as ever because you still need deep domain understanding to get the most out of agents. But now the ability to deliver on projects has a 10X multiplier. This means that you can make clients happier, compete to win more of them, go after smaller customers not in the TAM before, or deliver outcomes that weren’t really conceivable.

This is going to happen in advertising, IT transformation, management consulting, finance, and a number of other fields that historically are just fully constrained by the speed of their workforce for output. 

This is a huge opportunity right now for those starting these firms. I wouldn’t count out existing players that commit to the transformation either as existing customer trust goes a long way. But they have to move quickly to make it work.

Coding gives you a window into what the future will look like for a large amount of knowledge work. 

The first step for most jobs is that we go from doing most of the research, typing, and value creation manually (even if it’s using digital tools) to soon coordinating the work that agents are doing. 

Next, as this step itself becomes redundant or slows down what agents are capable of, we will be giving agents goals to optimize against and they’ll go off on and increasingly solve larger problems for us. 

This may at first blush look like something whose impact gets stuck with coding, but actually a large percentage of knowledge work may eventually just converge with this form factor due to the massive productivity gains that can be generated. Agents will use computers, leverage our existing tools or write new ones, and write code on the fly to solve larger swaths of knowledge work. 

So even if a task today doesn’t seem to be “coding” directly, the task may eventually fold into being coding adjacent. Manufacturing, architecture, life sciences, material sciences, cyber, and on and on.
 
One big hurdle in the way ultimately will be that much of this work remains non-verifiable, so humans will be even more in the loop than they are in coding. But the part that they can hand off will just get bigger and bigger over time as the models are more capable.

So in short, pay attention to coding and you’ll get a sense for where work is going.

This wouldn’t have sounded possible a year ago, but it’s becoming much more reasonable now that you can get 10X output gains based on the latest in AI model and harness progress. The result is that teams within the same company are driving very different levels of output based on how they’ve adopted AI.

This is a different phenomenon from other tech. Typically in the economy you think of technology adoption rates on a per firm basis, because the company generally adopts a relatively standardized approach to doing the new tech thing. Like “that company has gone digital or adopted the cloud”. So generally the uplift across teams is more or less the same across teams. 

AI is starting to look quite different. Even within the same company you can have a 10X delta between the lowest and highest adopters of AI and the impact they’re seeing. The teams that are able to actually figure out how to redesign their processes to best deploy agents in their workflows can see up to an order of magnitude jump in productivity depending on the job function.

Right now this is heavily concentrated in coding, but more work will become coding adjacent so we can expect similar results elsewhere too. This is going to definitely lead to some wild dynamics within companies.

This is a pretty key insight. Services businesses are always held back by their ability to deliver outcomes to customers. 

That scaling essentially only could come from headcount, and no matter how much demand you saw, there was always a finite amount of talent you could get for the problem you were going after. Not to mention, the customer generally always wants the work done faster, at a lower price, or at a higher quality.

Agents entirely change the calculus here, because now we can scale output in a way that’s decoupled from the among of time that goes in. A single engineer can have the output of dozens of engineers before. A single designer can probably build out your entire design system and brand. And so on.

Well why isn’t this just all agents then? Because the key is to still have experts on the front end that actually can ensure the right outcomes are delivered from agents.

It’s likely that we’re going to see this in a wide variety of categories. You’ll see this in cyber security, advertising and marketing, legal, accounting, IT transformation, and a number of other historically people-only services industries.

It’s a great time if you’re starting one of these businesses, or if you have the capability to transform an existing one.

AI native teams will eventually force the surrounding organization to become AI native too.

Take software development. coding velocity is way up thanks to AI, while actual shipped products and business impact are unchanged in most companies. That’s cos the surrounding system of experimentation tooling, evaluation, launch processes, and gtm are outdated.

It’s like sticking a Ferrari engine in a sedan and racing it on Indian roads. The engine can rev faster but the car speed is limited by its system and environment.

AI native companies were built ground up for this new way of building and shipping. They’re also able to shed suboptimal processes faster.

Market forces will quickly force all companies to adapt or perish.

If you’re solving this for your company: map out your product lifecycle and rebuild it ground up - tooling, team structure, gtm, everything.

tweets.text:
12 tips for people who posted on LinkedIn but now wanna post on X

A lot of people I know are moving their posting from LinkedIn to X. When they ask me how I grew 80k followers on X in one year, here’s what I tell them:

1. LinkedIn is a stage. X is a party. First you find your crowd, then you listen to what they're already talking about. Don't start talking until you get it

2. You can't reach the C-suite directly. LinkedIn is a professional network, so you can go straight to decision makers. X doesn't work like that. You have to get mass attention first, and then the right people notice you

3. Post way more than you think. On LinkedIn, 3-5 posts a week counts as a lot. I posted 3 times a day on X for 6 months. Some founders I follow post 5 times a day. It's not that they're on X all day. They just don't overthink it

4. Make posting a reflex. If you spend too long on a post, you won't post. Whenever a thought comes up, post it right there. No planning, no scheduling, no waiting for the right time

5. It's a numbers game. Most posts won't do well. Maybe 1 in 10 will. Maybe 1 in 50 goes viral. That's normal

6. Half your posts should be reactions. LinkedIn is mostly “proactive content”. On X, at least at the start, half of what you post should be “reactive content”: replies, quote tweets, commentary on what others already said

7. Know the difference between a reply and a quote tweet. A reply is like a LinkedIn DM. It says "notice me." A quote tweet uses someone else's content to grow your own account

8. Fix your feed first. If you wanna talk about cybersecurity and your feed is all politics, you can't join the right conversations. Pick a few big names in your niche. See who they follow and who they engage with, and follow those people too. Like, bookmark and comment. After about a week your timeline will look totally different

9. Write like you're texting an acquaintance. Polish turns people off. Everyone's allergic to perfect AI-sounding writing. And please don't use AI or bots to write your replies. People can tell, and they might block you

10. Post the stuff that's obvious to you. Make a list of the top 10 questions customers, investors and your team ask you. That's where you're the expert. What seems too obvious to talk about is exactly what people want to hear

11. Post what you just said out loud. If you say something in real life and people go "huh, never thought of it that way," post it on your way back. Don't wait, you'll forget. You don't have to block out time to think of what to say. Just say what you've already said

12. Show your face, and don't sell yet. X is a wall of text, so video stands out. I just record myself on my laptop with something on the screen. People wanna know you're a real human, not AI slop. And until you have about 1,000 followers, don't promote your company. Share real opinions first. Later, when you repost company news, always add your own take, not PR speak.

Remember: people follow people, not companies
